pos: n. (bodily craving; rendering Hebrew nephesh, the soul)
etymology: From Latin appetere, to seek after. The Hebrew simply says soul — which is why Scripture treats appetite as a matter of the whole person.
biblical_def: Appetite is craving. Proverbs treats it as something to be governed at table: “When thou sittest to eat with a ruler, consider diligently what is before thee: and put a knife to thy throat, if thou be a man given to appetite” (Pro 23:1–2). Ecclesiastes notes that “all the labour of man is for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled” (Ecc 6:7), and Isaiah pictures the hungry man who dreams he eats and wakes “and his soul is empty” (Isa 29:8). Paul warns of those “whose God is their belly” (Php 3:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines appetite as the natural desire of pleasure or good; and a desire of food or drink; a painful sensation occasioned by hunger.
webster_full: APPETITE, n. The natural desire of pleasure or good; the desire of gratification, either of the body or of the mind.
2. A desire of food or drink; a painful sensation occasioned by hunger.
3. Strong desire; eagerness or longing.
scriptures: Pro 23:1
When thou sittest to eat with a ruler, consider diligently what is before thee:
Pro 23:2
And put a knife to thy throat, if thou be a man given to appetite.
Ecc 6:7
All the labour of man is for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled.
Php 3:19
Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.)
corruption_summary: Appetite is either indulged as identity or fought as an enemy, when Proverbs treats it as a servant that must be governed most carefully in the presence of power.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 23:1-3 is oddly specific about the setting: when thou sittest to eat with a ruler, consider diligently what is before thee. The warning is not about gluttony in general but about appetite at a powerful man's table, where dainties are described as deceitful meat. A man whose appetites are visible to those who can feed them is a man who can be bought, and the price is often just a good dinner and the feeling of having arrived.

Ecclesiastes 6:7 states the structural problem: all the labour of man is for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled. Appetite is designed to recur, which makes it an excellent servant and a hopeless master — no quantity closes the account. Philippians names the end state without cruelty but without softening either: whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.
roots_summary: Hebrew nephesh (H5315), soul, life, appetite — the same word for the whole person and for its cravings; Greek koilia (G2836), belly.
roots_lines: Hebrew nephesh (H5315) — soul, desire, appetite; Proverbs 23:2, Ecclesiastes 6:7, Isaiah 29:8.
Greek koilia (G2836) — belly; Philippians 3:19, Romans 16:18, they serve their own belly.
Greek epithumia (G1939) — desire, lust; the New Testament's broader word for craving.
usage: “Put a knife to thy throat, if thou be a man given to appetite” — govern it at a ruler's table.
“The appetite is not filled” — designed to recur, hopeless as a master.
“Whose God is their belly” — the end state named plainly.

etymology: Old English ofthyrst, thoroughly thirsty. The intensive prefix survives in the KJV's form.
biblical_def: Athirst means thirsty. Samson, having just won a victory, nearly dies of it and calls on God (Jdg 15:18). Ruth is told to drink from the young men's vessels “when thou art athirst” (Rut 2:9). Christ says from the cross, “I thirst” (Joh 19:28), and the Bible's last invitation uses the word: “let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely” (Rev 22:17). The only qualification named is the thirst itself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines athirst as thirsty, wanting drink; and figuratively, having a keen appetite or desire.
webster_full: ATHIRST, a. Thirsty; wanting drink.
2. Having a keen appetite or desire.
scriptures: And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.

And he was sore athirst, and called on the LORD, and said, Thou hast given this great deliverance into the hand of thy servant: and now shall I die for thirst, and fall into the hand of the uncircumcised?
Rut 2:9

Let thine eyes be on the field that they do reap, and go thou after them: have I not charged the young men that they shall not touch thee? and when thou art athirst, go unto the vessels, and drink of that which the young men have drawn.
After this, Jesus knowing that all things were now accomplished, that the scripture might be fulfilled, saith, I thirst.
corruption_summary: Invitations to Christ get hedged with qualifications He never states, when Revelation's final call asks only for thirst and willingness.
corruption_paragraphs: Revelation 22:17 is the last invitation in the Bible and its terms are the plainest anywhere: let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely. There is no preparation demanded, no threshold of sincerity specified, no prior improvement required. The qualification is a need and a willingness, and the price is stated as freely. Every additional condition a preacher adds is his own.

Judges 15:18 is worth keeping beside it because it shows thirst arriving at the worst moment. Samson had just killed a thousand men with the jawbone of an ass, and immediately he was sore athirst, and called on the LORD, and said, Thou hast given this great deliverance into the hand of thy servant: and now shall I die for thirst? Victory does not exempt anyone from need, and the strongest man in Scripture had to ask for water like everyone else.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsame (H6771), thirsty; Greek dipsao (G1372), to thirst — the verb of the beatitude, blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsame (H6771) — thirsty; Judges 15:18, Ruth 2:9, Psalm 42:2, my soul thirsteth for God.
Greek dipsao (G1372) — to thirst; Matthew 5:6, John 4:14, 7:37, Revelation 22:17.
Greek dorean (G1432) — freely, without cost; the price named in the final invitation.
usage: “Let him that is athirst come” — the only qualification is the thirst.
“Shall I die for thirst?” — Samson needy in the hour of victory.
“When thou art athirst, go unto the vessels” — Boaz's provision for Ruth.

pos: n. (affliction, hard circumstance; rendering Hebrew tsarah and ra)
etymology: From Latin adversitas, from adversus, turned against. Adversity is circumstance facing the wrong way.
biblical_def: Adversity is affliction. Proverbs makes it diagnostic of strength: “If thou faint in the day of adversity, thy strength is small” (Pro 24:10), and of friendship: “A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity” (Pro 17:17). Ecclesiastes sets the two seasons side by side as equally appointed: “In the day of prosperity be joyful, but in the day of adversity consider: God also hath set the one over against the other” (Ecc 7:14). Hebrews commands remembrance of “them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body” (Heb 13:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines adversity as an event or series of events which oppose success or desire; misfortune; calamity; affliction; distress; state of unhappiness.
webster_full: ADVERSITY, n. An event, or series of events, which oppose success or desire; misfortune; calamity; affliction; distress; state of unhappiness.
scriptures: If thou faint in the day of adversity, thy strength is small.
A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
Ecc 7:14
In the day of prosperity be joyful, but in the day of adversity consider: God also hath set the one over against the other, to the end that man should find nothing after him.
Heb 13:3
Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body.
corruption_summary: Hard seasons are read as diagnostic of God's displeasure or of insufficient faith, when Ecclesiastes says He sets prosperity and adversity deliberately over against each other.
corruption_paragraphs: Ecclesiastes 7:14 is the verse that dismantles both prosperity teaching and its despairing opposite: in the day of prosperity be joyful, but in the day of adversity consider: God also hath set the one over against the other, to the end that man should find nothing after him. Both seasons are appointed, and they are deliberately alternated so that no one can read his circumstances as a reliable index of God's disposition toward him. The instruction for the good day is enjoy; for the bad day, consider.

Proverbs 17:17 supplies the social remedy, and the second clause is stronger than it first sounds: a brother is born for adversity. Not merely useful in it — born for it. Some relationships exist precisely for the seasons when nothing can be fixed and someone simply has to be there. Hebrews 13:3 gives the reason a church must practise this: remember them… which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body. You are made of the same material.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsarah (H6869), distress, trouble — from a root meaning narrowness; ra (H7451), evil or calamity; Greek kakoucheo (G2558), to be ill-treated.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsarah (H6869) — distress, adversity; Proverbs 17:17, Psalm 46:1, a very present help in trouble.
Hebrew ra (H7451) — evil, calamity; Ecclesiastes 7:14, the day of adversity.
Greek kakoucheo (G2558) — to suffer adversity, be ill-treated; Hebrews 11:37 and 13:3.
usage: “If thou faint in the day of adversity, thy strength is small” — the day is a measurement.
“A brother is born for adversity” — some relationships exist for this.
“God also hath set the one over against the other” — both seasons appointed.

pos: n. (a feast; rendering Hebrew mishteh, a drinking)
etymology: From Italian banchetto, a little bench — a meal taken at table. The Hebrew word means a drinking, since wine defined the occasion.
biblical_def: A banquet is a feast. Esther's two banquets frame the reversal of Haman's plot — she petitions the king only at the second (Est 5:4–8; 7:2). The Song makes it an image of love's shelter: “He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love” (Son 2:4). Amos condemns those at ease whose “banquet of them that stretched themselves shall be removed” (Amo 6:7), and Peter files banquetings among what the Gentiles walk in (1Pe 4:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines banquet as a feast; a rich entertainment of meat and drink; and as a verb, to treat with a feast, to feast.
webster_full: BANQUET, n. A feast; a rich entertainment of meat and drink.
BANQUET, v.t. To treat with a feast or rich entertainment.
BANQUET, v.i. To feast; to regale one's self with good eating and drinking.
scriptures: Est 5:4
And Esther answered, If it seem good unto the king, let the king and Haman come this day unto the banquet that I have prepared for him.
Son 2:4
He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love.
Amo 6:7
Therefore now shall they go captive with the first that go captive, and the banquet of them that stretched themselves shall be removed.
For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries:
corruption_summary: Feasting is treated as either worldly or trivial, while Scripture uses it for both the height of danger and the picture of covenant love.
corruption_paragraphs: Esther's strategy repays study. Invited to name her request, with the king offering up to half the kingdom, she asks only that he and Haman come to another banquet. The delay is not indecision; it is timing. Between the two feasts falls the sleepless night in which the king reads the chronicles and discovers Mordecai's unrewarded service, and Haman builds a gallows he will hang on. Esther's patience allowed providence to arrange the room before she spoke.

Song 2:4 gives the other use, and the second clause is the point: he brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love. A banner is a public standard, raised where everyone can see it. The image is not of private affection but of a love declared over someone in the open — which is how a covenant differs from a feeling.
roots_summary: Hebrew mishteh (H4960), a feast or drinking; Greek potos (G4224), a drinking bout, in 1 Peter 4:3.
roots_lines: Hebrew mishteh (H4960) — feast, banquet; Esther 5:4-8, 7:2, Daniel 5:10.
Hebrew yayin (H3196) — wine; the banquet of wine in Esther 7:2.
Greek potos (G4224) — carousing, banqueting; only 1 Peter 4:3.
usage: “Let the king and Haman come this day unto the banquet” — timing that let providence work.
“His banner over me was love” — affection declared in the open.
“The banquet of them that stretched themselves shall be removed” — Amos on ease.

pos: n. (generosity, a liberal gift; rendering Greek eulogia, blessing)
etymology: From Latin bonitas, goodness. Bounty is goodness in the form of a gift — character made transferable.
biblical_def: Bounty is generous giving. Paul uses it of the Corinthian collection, sending brethren ahead so the gift would be ready “as a matter of bounty, and not as of covetousness” (2Co 9:5) — prepared willingly rather than extracted under pressure. Solomon's wealth is described as given him “of his royal bounty” to the queen of Sheba (1Ki 10:13). The principle attached is agricultural: “he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully” (2Co 9:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines bounty as liberality in bestowing gifts and favors; generosity; munificence.
webster_full: BOUNTY, n. Liberality in bestowing gifts and favors; generosity; munificence.
2. A premium offered or given to induce men to enlist into the public service.
3. A premium for encouraging any branch of industry.
scriptures: Therefore I thought it necessary to exhort the brethren, that they would go before unto you, and make up beforehand your bounty, whereof ye had notice before, that the same might be ready, as a matter of bounty, and not as of covetousness.
But this I say, He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully.
Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.

And king Solomon gave unto the queen of Sheba all her desire, whatsoever she asked, beside that which Solomon gave her of his royal bounty. So she turned and went to her own country, she and her servants. of
corruption_summary: Christian giving is engineered by appeal and urgency, which 2 Corinthians 9 calls covetousness rather than bounty — the same money, extracted the wrong way.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Corinthians 9:5 draws a distinction that most fundraising erases. Paul sends brethren ahead to prepare the gift beforehand, so that it may be ready as a matter of bounty, and not as of covetousness. The identical sum is bounty when planned freely and covetousness when squeezed out on the day by an effective appeal. He is careful to arrive after the collection is complete precisely so his presence cannot function as pressure.

Verse 7 supplies the rule and the reason: every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver. Purpose comes first, then the giving, and the manner matters to God as much as the amount. That single verse rules out both the guilt-driven gift and the impulsive one, and leaves a discipline that is harder and far more freeing than either.
roots_summary: Greek eulogia (G2129), blessing, bounty — the word for a generous gift; hilaros (G2431), cheerful, the giver God loves.
roots_lines: Greek eulogia (G2129) — blessing, bounty; 2 Corinthians 9:5, twice in one verse.
Greek pleonexia (G4124) — covetousness, extortion; the contrast Paul draws in the same verse.
Greek hilaros (G2431) — cheerful; 2 Corinthians 9:7, God loveth a cheerful giver.
usage: “As a matter of bounty, and not as of covetousness” — same sum, different extraction.
“He which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully” — the agricultural rule.
“Not grudgingly, or of necessity” — the manner matters to God.

pos: n. (a good received; rendering Hebrew gemul, Greek euergesia)
etymology: From Latin bene facere, to do well. A benefit is a good deed viewed from the side of the one who received it.
biblical_def: A benefit is a good received. The psalmist's cure for a sluggish soul is to count them: “Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits” (Psa 103:2) — and the list follows: forgiveness, healing, redemption, crowning, satisfying, renewal. He also asks the accounting question: “What shall I render unto the LORD for all his benefits toward me?” (Psa 116:12). Hezekiah is faulted because “he rendered not again according to the benefit done unto him” (2Ch 32:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines benefit as an act of kindness; a favor conferred; and advantage, profit, or a natural advantage.
webster_full: BENEFIT, n. An act of kindness; a favor conferred.
2. Advantage; profit; a word of extensive use, and expressing whatever contributes to promote prosperity and personal happiness.
3. In law, benefit of clergy.
scriptures: Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits:
What shall I render unto the LORD for all his benefits toward me?
But Hezekiah rendered not again according to the benefit done unto him; for his heart was lifted up: therefore there was wrath upon him, and upon Judah and Jerusalem.
Blessed be the Lord, who daily loadeth us with benefits, even the God of our salvation. Selah.
corruption_summary: Gratitude is treated as a mood that arrives, when the psalmist treats it as an act of memory performed deliberately against a forgetful soul.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 103:2 is an instruction addressed to oneself, and the verb is negative: forget not all his benefits. The psalmist knows his own soul will default to forgetting, so he speaks to it — bless the LORD, O my soul — and then supplies a specific list rather than a general sentiment: who forgiveth all thine iniquities; who healeth all thy diseases; who redeemeth thy life from destruction. Gratitude here is a discipline of enumeration, not a feeling waited upon.

2 Chronicles 32:25 records what happens when the accounting is not kept. Hezekiah had been healed after praying, and given a sign; but Hezekiah rendered not again according to the benefit done unto him; for his heart was lifted up. Deliverance received without gratitude curdles into entitlement, and the very mercy that should have humbled him became the occasion of his pride.
roots_summary: Hebrew gemul (H1576), a dealing or recompense; tagmul (H8408), benefit, in Psalm 116:12; Greek euergesia (G2108), a good deed done.
roots_lines: Hebrew gemul (H1576) — dealing, benefit, recompense; Psalm 103:2, 2 Chronicles 32:25.
Hebrew tagmul (H8408) — benefit; only Psalm 116:12, what shall I render.
Greek euergesia (G2108) — good deed, benefit; Acts 4:9, 1 Timothy 6:2.
usage: “Forget not all his benefits” — gratitude as deliberate enumeration.
“What shall I render unto the LORD?” — the accounting question.
“Rendered not again according to the benefit” — mercy curdled into pride.

pos: n. (one who asks alms; rendering Hebrew ebyon, Greek ptochos)
etymology: From beg, of uncertain origin. The Greek ptochos means one who crouches — destitution visible in posture.
biblical_def: A beggar lives by alms. Hannah's song announces God's characteristic reversal: “He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes, and to make them inherit the throne of glory” (1Sa 2:8). Lazarus lies at the rich man's gate and is carried by angels into Abraham's bosom (Luk 16:20–22). Blind Bartimaeus sits by the wayside begging and will not be silenced (Mar 10:46–48). Christ's first beatitude blesses the ptochos in spirit (Mat 5:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a beggar as one that lives by asking alms, or makes it his business to beg; and one who supplicates with humility.
webster_full: BEGGAR, n. One that lives by asking alms, or makes it his business to beg.
2. One who supplicates with humility; a petitioner.
3. One who assumes in argument what he does not prove.
scriptures: He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes, and to make them inherit the throne of glory: for the pillars of the earth are the LORD'S, and he hath set the world upon them.
And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, which was laid at his gate, full of sores,
And they came to Jericho: and as he went out of Jericho with his disciples and a great number of people, blind Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus, sat by the highway side begging.
Mat 5:3
Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
corruption_summary: Poverty is read as a problem to be managed at a distance, while Scripture keeps putting a named beggar at a named gate and making the response the test.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 16 gives the beggar a name and leaves the rich man anonymous, which reverses every social record ever kept. Lazarus is named; the rich man is described only by his clothing and his table. The gate is the detail that convicts: the beggar was laid daily at his gate, so the rich man's failure was not ignorance but proximity managed into invisibility. He knew the name after death — send Lazarus — which proves he had known it all along.

Mark 10 shows the beggar who refuses to be hushed. Many charged Bartimaeus that he should hold his peace: but he cried the more a great deal, Thou son of David, have mercy on me. The crowd's instinct was to keep the noise away from Christ; Christ's response was stand still, and call him. And the first thing the healed man did was follow Jesus in the way, which is what beggars do when they discover who has been listening.
roots_summary: Hebrew ebyon (H34), needy, poor; Greek ptochos (G4434), a crouching beggar — the word of the first beatitude, poor in spirit.
roots_lines: Hebrew ebyon (H34) — needy, beggar; 1 Samuel 2:8, Psalm 113:7, he raiseth up the poor out of the dust.
Greek ptochos (G4434) — beggar, destitute; Luke 16:20, 22, Matthew 5:3.
Greek prosaiteo (G4319) — to beg; Mark 10:46, blind Bartimaeus sat by the highway side begging.
usage: “Lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes” — God's characteristic reversal.
“Laid at his gate” — proximity managed into invisibility.
“He cried the more a great deal” — the beggar who would not be hushed.

pos: n. pl. (gifts given to pervert judgment; rendering Hebrew shochad)
etymology: From Old French bribe, a scrap given to a beggar. The word drifted from charity to corruption — a gift that buys a decision.
biblical_def: Bribes are gifts that pervert judgment. The law is blunt about their effect: “thou shalt take no gift: for the gift blindeth the wise, and perverteth the words of the righteous” (Exo 23:8). Samuel's sons “took bribes, and perverted judgment” (1Sa 8:3), which is the stated reason Israel demanded a king. Isaiah's portrait of the man who shall dwell on high includes one who “shaketh his hands from holding of bribes” (Isa 33:15), and God Himself “taketh not reward” (Deu 10:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bribe as a price, reward, gift or favor bestowed or promised with a view to pervert the judgment or corrupt the conduct of a judge, witness or other person.
webster_full: BRIBE, n. A price, reward, gift or favor bestowed or promised with a view to pervert the judgment, or corrupt the conduct of a judge, witness or other person.
2. That which seduces.
scriptures: Exo 23:8
And thou shalt take no gift: for the gift blindeth the wise, and perverteth the words of the righteous. the
And his sons walked not in his ways, but turned aside after lucre, and took bribes, and perverted judgment.

He that walketh righteously, and speaketh uprightly; he that despiseth the gain of oppressions, that shaketh his hands from holding of bribes, that stoppeth his ears from hearing of blood, and shutteth his eyes from seeing evil;
For the LORD your God is God of gods, and Lord of lords, a great God, a mighty, and a terrible, which regardeth not persons, nor taketh reward:
corruption_summary: Modern bribery arrives as access, sponsorship, and favours between friends, and Exodus names its effect precisely — it blinds the wise, who never notice they have stopped seeing.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 23:8 is careful about who is at risk: the gift blindeth the wise, and perverteth the words of the righteous. Not the foolish and the wicked — the wise and the righteous. That is the whole danger. A corrupt man does not need a bribe to rule badly; a good man needs one, and once received it operates below the level of conscious decision. He does not decide to favour his benefactor; he simply finds his arguments more persuasive.

1 Samuel 8:3 shows the institutional consequence. Samuel's sons walked not in his ways, but turned aside after lucre, and took bribes, and perverted judgment — and the elders of Israel used exactly this to demand a king like all the nations. Corruption in the second generation of a godly leadership does more damage than open opposition ever did, because it discredits the arrangement itself.
roots_summary: Hebrew shochad (H7810), a gift given to secure favour or pervert justice; the verb shachad, to bribe.
roots_lines: Hebrew shochad (H7810) — bribe, gift; Exodus 23:8, Deuteronomy 16:19, 1 Samuel 8:3, Isaiah 33:15.
Hebrew betsa (H1215) — unjust gain, lucre; 1 Samuel 8:3, turned aside after lucre.
Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, justice; what the bribe perverts.
usage: “The gift blindeth the wise” — the wise and righteous are the ones at risk.
“Took bribes, and perverted judgment” — why Israel demanded a king.
“Shaketh his hands from holding of bribes” — the man who dwells on high.

pos: n. (self-formed opinion; rendering Hebrew ayin, in one's own eyes)
etymology: From Latin concipere, to conceive. A conceit is an opinion conceived in oneself — and Scripture's concern is that it was never fathered by anything outside.
biblical_def: A conceit is a self-generated estimate. Proverbs regards it as more hopeless than folly: “Seest thou a man wise in his own conceit? there is more hope of a fool than of him” (Pro 26:12), and again, “The sluggard is wiser in his own conceit than seven men that can render a reason” (Pro 26:16). Paul warns the Roman Gentiles, “be not wise in your own conceits” (Rom 12:16), and repeats it about Israel's blindness lest the church grow proud (Rom 11:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conceit as conception, that which is conceived or formed in the mind; and an opinion of one's own importance; self-flattering opinion.
webster_full: CONCEIT, n. Conception; that which is conceived, imagined or formed in the mind; idea; thought; image.
2. Understanding; power of conceiving.
3. Opinion; notion; fancy.
4. Pleasant fancy; gaiety of imagination.
5. Favorable or self-flattering opinion; a lofty conception of one's own qualities.
scriptures: Seest thou a man wise in his own conceit? there is more hope of a fool than of him.
The sluggard is wiser in his own conceit than seven men that can render a reason.
Be of the same mind one toward another. Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate. Be not wise in your own conceits.

For I would not, brethren, that ye should be ignorant of this mystery, lest ye should be wise in your own conceits; that blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in.
corruption_summary: Confidence is trained and calibration is not, producing people whose certainty rises exactly as their competence falls — which is Proverbs 26:16 in a sentence.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 26:12 makes a ranking that ought to unsettle capable people: seest thou a man wise in his own conceit? there is more hope of a fool than of him. The fool at least may discover his folly; the self-satisfied man has closed the only door through which correction enters. This is why Scripture treats teachability as a more reliable sign of wisdom than any demonstration of knowledge.

Verse 16 adds the comic and painful detail: the sluggard is wiser in his own conceit than seven men that can render a reason. The least productive man in the chapter has the highest opinion of his own judgment, and he holds it against seven men who can actually argue their case. Conceit is inversely related to output, which is why it survives — it never gets tested.
roots_summary: Hebrew be-enav, in his own eyes — the recurring Proverbs idiom; Greek phronimos par heautois, wise with themselves, in Romans 12:16.
roots_lines: Hebrew ayin (H5869) — eye; the idiom wise in his own eyes, Proverbs 26:12, 16, 3:7.
Greek phronimos (G5429) — prudent, wise; Romans 12:16, be not wise in your own conceits.
Greek huperphroneo (G5252) — to think too highly; Romans 12:3, not to think of himself more highly than he ought.
usage: “More hope of a fool than of him” — conceit closes the door correction enters by.
“Wiser in his own conceit than seven men that can render a reason” — certainty untested.
“Be not wise in your own conceits” — addressed to a church, not to pagans.

pos: n. (one who shares bread and way; rendering Hebrew chaber, Greek koinonos)
etymology: From Latin com with and panis bread — a companion is literally one you eat bread with.
biblical_def: A companion is one who shares the road. The psalmist chooses his deliberately: “I am a companion of all them that fear thee, and of them that keep thy precepts” (Psa 119:63). Proverbs warns of the alternative: “he that is a companion of riotous men shameth his father” (Pro 28:7), and “a companion of fools shall be destroyed” (Pro 13:20). David's bitterest complaint is of one who was “a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance” (Psa 55:13), and John calls himself the churches' “companion in tribulation” (Rev 1:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a companion as one who keeps company with another; one with whom a person frequently associates and converses.
webster_full: COMPANION, n. One who keeps company with another; one with whom a person frequently associates, and converses.
2. A partner; an associate.
3. A fellow; a mate.
scriptures: I am a companion of all them that fear thee, and of them that keep thy precepts.
He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.
But it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance.
Rev 1:9

I John, who also am your brother, and companion in tribulation, and in the kingdom and patience of Jesus Christ, was in the isle that is called Patmos, for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ.
corruption_summary: Friendship is treated as a matter of chemistry rather than choice, when Psalm 119 records a deliberate decision about whose company to keep.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 119:63 states a policy, not a preference: I am a companion of all them that fear thee, and of them that keep thy precepts. The criterion is neither temperament nor shared interests but a common fear of God and obedience to His word, and the word all makes it wide — anyone who meets that test is included, whatever else divides them. That is a far better basis for church fellowship than the affinity groupings congregations usually fall into.

Proverbs 13:20 states the mechanism with no room for exceptions: he that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed. Character is transmitted by proximity, in both directions, and neither transmission requires anyone's consent. Revelation 1:9 shows the highest form of it — John, your brother, and companion in tribulation, and in the kingdom and patience of Jesus Christ. Some companionship is defined by what is suffered together.
roots_summary: Hebrew chaber (H2270), an associate, companion; Greek koinonos (G2844), a partner or sharer — the same root as fellowship.
roots_lines: Hebrew chaber (H2270) — companion, associate; Psalm 119:63, Ecclesiastes 4:10.
Greek koinonos (G2844) — partner, sharer; 2 Corinthians 1:7, partakers of the sufferings.
Greek sugkoinonos (G4791) — joint partaker; Revelation 1:9, your companion in tribulation.
usage: “I am a companion of all them that fear thee” — a policy, not a preference.
“A companion of fools shall be destroyed” — transmission requires no consent.
“Your brother, and companion in tribulation” — fellowship defined by shared suffering.
